Determining habitat anomalies in cross-diffusion predator-prey chemotaxis models

Yuhan Li Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, P. R. China Affiliation: yuhli2-c@my.cityu.edu.hk    Hongyu Liu Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, P. R. China    Catharine W. K. Lo Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, Shenzhen University, Shenzhen, 518061, P.R. China Affiliation: hongyliu@cityu.edu.hk, hongyu.liuip@gmail.com Affiliation: catharinelowk@gmail.com, cwklo@szu.edu.cn
Abstract

This paper addresses an open inverse problem at the interface of mathematical analysis and spatial ecology: the unique identification of unknown spatial anomalies – interpreted as zones of habitat degradation – and their associated ecological parameters in multi-species predator-prey systems with multiple chemical signals, using only boundary measurements. We formulate the problem as the simultaneous recovery of an unknown interior subdomain and the discontinuous ecological interaction rules across its boundary. A unified theoretical framework is developed that uniquely determines both the anomaly’s geometry and the discontinuous coefficients characterizing the altered interactions within the degraded region. Our results cover smooth anomalies in time-dependent systems and are extended to non-smooth polyhedral inclusions in stationary regimes. This work bridges a gap between ecological sensing and the quantitative inference of internal habitat heterogeneity, offering a mathematical basis for detecting and characterizing habitat degradation from limited external data.  

Keywords: Inverse boundary value problems; multi-species cross-diffusion predator-prey chemotaxis models; habitat degradation; anomaly detection; unique identifiability. 
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 35R30, 35Q92, 92-10, 92D25, 35R35

1 Introduction

1.1 Biology background and motivation of our study

The intricate dynamics governing how cohabiting species interact with each other and their heterogeneous environments represent a cornerstone of spatial ecology. Real-world populations are distributed across landscapes fragmented by spatial anomalies such as zones of habitat degradation, where resource availability, toxicity, or physical structure differ sharply from the surrounding environment. To capture the resulting dynamics, models must account for both random dispersal and the directed movement of organisms in response to environmental cues across these discontinuous domains.

A fundamental mechanism for such directed movement is chemotaxis [12, 2, 3], the ability to sense and move along chemical gradients. This process is central to diverse ecological functions and is acutely sensitive to habitat degradation, which can disrupt chemical signaling pathways. For instance, in soil ecosystems, chemotaxis drives essential microbial processes like nitrogen fixation and denitrification, where contamination or pH shifts can sever these chemical dialogues. Similarly, in the mammalian gut, chemotaxis underpins the complex spatial organization of the microbiota; inflammation or antibiotic exposure can degrade this chemical landscape, leading to dysbiosis. By integrating such taxis mechanisms, models bridge the scale from local individual interactions to the emergent, large-scale spatial patterns – and their disruption – observed in nature.

A powerful framework that integrates interspecies dynamics with spatial movement is the predator-prey chemotaxis system, which models interactions where movement is directed by chemical stimuli, typically a chemoattractant produced by the prey. An illustrative formulation, extending both the classic Lotka-Volterra predator-prey framework and the Keller-Segel chemotaxis paradigm [14, 34, 1, 32], is given by:

{∂tu=duΔu−χ∇⋅(u∇w)−auv,∂tv=dv​Δ​v+b​u​v−c​v,∂tw=dw​Δ​w+d​u−e​w,\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=d_{u}\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w)-auv,\\ \partial_{t}v=d_{v}\Delta v+buv-cv,\\ \partial_{t}w=d_{w}\Delta w+du-ew,\end{cases} (1.1)

where u⁡(x,t)u(x,t), v⁡(x,t)v(x,t), and w⁡(x,t)w(x,t) denote the densities of prey, predator, and chemoattractant, respectively. The parameters du,dv,dwd_{u},d_{v},d_{w} are diffusion coefficients; χ\chi is the prey’s chemotactic sensitivity; and a,b,c,d,ea,b,c,d,e represent predation rate, predator growth, predator mortality, chemoattractant production, and its degradation. Critically, in a degraded zone, parameters such as the predation rate aa or chemotactic sensitivity χ\chi may change discontinuously, modeling a sharp shift in ecological rules.

In this system, the dynamics has been further enriched by incorporating prey-taxis, which describes directed movement of prey in response to predator gradients or conspecifics [8, 33, 27, 37, 22]. This mechanism, introduced by [13] and developed by [12], is crucial for modeling adaptive anti-predator strategies. For example, predatory bacteria like Bdellovibrio exhibit prey-taxis towards chemical signals from Escherichia coli prey. Such behavior can be modeled by adding a term χ∇⋅(u∇u)\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla u) for self-aggregation or −χ∇⋅(u∇v)-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v) for predator-avoidance. These strategies are themselves vulnerable to disruption in degraded habitats.

Beyond taxis, cross-diffusion provides another essential mechanism for spatial pattern formation. Pioneered by Shigesada, Kawasaki, and Teramoto [31], it generalizes dispersal by allowing the population gradient of one species to directly influence the movement of another:

{∂tu=∇⋅(du∇u+d1∇v),∂tv=∇⋅(dv∇v+d2∇u).\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=\nabla\cdot(d_{u}\nabla u+d_{1}\nabla v),\\ \partial_{t}v=\nabla\cdot(d_{v}\nabla v+d_{2}\nabla u).\end{cases}

Here, coefficients d1d_{1} and d2d_{2} quantify interspecific dispersal pressures. Their sign is ecologically significant: negative values typically induce aggregation, while positive values promote segregation. In a degraded anomaly, these cross-diffusive couplings may flip sign or change magnitude, representing a breakdown or reversal of typical spatial interactions [26, 7]. These dynamics are not merely theoretical; they are observed in complex microbial ecosystems, such as within biofilms, where interspecific chemical signaling can lead to attraction or repulsion, effectively manifesting as cross-diffusion and resulting in structured spatial organization.

In summary, these models form a sophisticated toolkit for forward modeling of population dynamics under spatial heterogeneity [19]. The pervasive nature of habitat degradation and other spatial anomalies necessitates robust methods not only to model their effects but, crucially, to detect and characterize them non-invasively. However, the corresponding inverse problem – deducing such anomalous subregions with discontinuous ecological rules from externally observed data – remains a significant open challenge in spatial ecology.

This leads to the central question of this work: How can one uniquely identify and localize a subregion of habitat degradation within a domain, and simultaneously quantify the discontinuous ecological interaction rules inside it, using only population data measured at the domain’s boundary over time?

In this paper, we address this inverse problem for a class of spatially extended ecological systems featuring cross-diffusion and taxis. Our objective is the simultaneous recovery of both the geometric shape of an internal anomaly – representing a zone of habitat degradation – and the set of altered ecological parameters within it. Mathematically, this is formulated as the unique determination of an unknown interior subdomain and the piecewise-constant or discontinuous coefficients that govern species interaction and movement across its boundary. This framework constitutes a significant departure from prior inverse problem studies in mathematical biology, which have largely been confined to the recovery of smoothly varying or globally constant parameters [17, 16, 18].

Our results establish a mathematical foundation for non-invasive ecological sensing. A direct application is the localization and characterization of a subsurface contaminant plume by observing the spatiotemporal response of microbial communities at the domain’s boundary. More broadly, the methodology is generalizable to a range of scenarios requiring the identification of hidden internal structures from boundary data, such as delineating strongholds of invasive species, detecting the onset of harmful algal blooms, or mapping regions of acute environmental stress within complex ecosystems.

1.2 Mathematical setup

Motivated by the works above, we consider the following multi-species, multi-chemical cross-diffusion predator-prey chemotaxis system with prey-taxis. Let the space-time domain be Q:=Ω×(0,T]Q:=\Omega\times(0,T] and its lateral boundary Σ:=∂Ω×(0,T]\Sigma:=\partial\Omega\times(0,T]. The governing system is given by:

In the long time limit T→∞T\to\infty, the system approaches a steady state in which transient dynamics decay and temporal derivatives become negligible relative to the diffusive, advective, and reactive terms. Consequently, the densities of prey species and chemical concentrations converge to time-independent equilibrium profiles, reducing the system to its stationary form:

Suppose there is an anomaly denoted by ω\omega, which is a subset of the habitat Ω\Omega. This anomaly corresponds to a distinct region within Ω\Omega, where the environmental conditions differ from the rest of the habitat. Specifically, this region might be either more hostile or more favorable for living. For example, it could have increased sunlight exposure or contain harmful chemicals and pesticides. Our objective is to identify and analyze this anomaly and its impact on the reaction functions FF and GG in equations (1.2) and (1.3), respectively.

We assume that ω\omega is an open bounded C2C^{2} domain within Ω\Omega, with Ω\ω\Omega\backslash\omega connected, and that the outer boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega is also of class C2C^{2} for Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. The reaction function 𝐆\mathbf{G} exhibits a discontinuity across ∂ω\partial\omega. Specifically, 𝐆\mathbf{G} takes the form

𝐆⁡(x,t,u1,…,uN,v1,…,vM)={𝐆1​(x,t,u1,…,uN,v1,…,vM)if​x∈ω,𝐆0​(x,t,u1,…,uN,v1,…,vM)otherwise,\mathbf{G}(x,t,u_{1},\dots,u_{N},v_{1},\dots,v_{M})=\begin{cases}\mathbf{G}^{1}(x,t,u_{1},\dots,u_{N},v_{1},\dots,v_{M})\quad&\text{if}\ x\in\omega,\\ \mathbf{G}^{0}(x,t,u_{1},\dots,u_{N},v_{1},\dots,v_{M})\quad&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (1.4)

with 𝐆1,𝐆0\mathbf{G}^{1},\mathbf{G}^{0} being CγC^{\gamma} Hölder continuous for some γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) in their respective domains, such that

𝐆1​(x,t,u1,…,uN,v1,…,vM)≠𝐆0​(x,t,u1,…,uN,v1,…,vM)for​x∈∂ω.\mathbf{G}^{1}(x,t,u_{1},\dots,u_{N},v_{1},\dots,v_{M})\neq\mathbf{G}^{0}(x,t,u_{1},\dots,u_{N},v_{1},\dots,v_{M})\quad\text{for}\ x\in\partial\omega. (1.5)

In the stationary case of equation (1.3), we similarly assume the presence of a topological structure characterized by an anomalous inhomogeneity ω⋐Ω\omega\Subset\Omega. Here, ω\omega is a bounded Lipschitz domain such that Ω\ω¯\Omega\backslash\bar{\omega} is connected. We also assume that a similar form holds for the reaction function 𝐅⁡(x,u1,…,uN,v1,…,vM)\mathbf{F}(x,u_{1},\dots,u_{N},v_{1},\dots,v_{M}), as in the time-dependent case for GG in (1.5). We will give more precise descriptions of these functions in subsection 3.2.

Associated to these inverse problems, we construct the following measurement maps of a pair of Cauchy data:

ℳω,𝐆+:=((𝐮,𝐯)|∂Ω,(𝐮,𝐯)|t=T)→ω,𝐆,\mathcal{M}^{+}_{\omega,\mathbf{G}}:=\left((\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})|_{\partial\Omega},(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})|_{t=T}\right)\to\omega,\mathbf{G}, (1.6)

where ν\nu is the exterior unit normal vector to ∂Ω\partial\Omega. Similarly, we have

ℳω,𝐅+:=(∂ν𝐮,∂ν𝐯)|∂Ω​ fixed→ω,𝐅,\mathcal{M}^{+}_{\omega,\mathbf{F}}:=(\partial_{\nu}\mathbf{u},\partial_{\nu}\mathbf{v})|_{\partial\Omega}\text{ fixed}\to\omega,\mathbf{F}, (1.7)

where 𝐟=(f1,…,fN)\mathbf{f}=(f_{1},\dots,f_{N}), 𝐠=(g1,…,gM)\mathbf{g}=(g_{1},\dots,g_{M}) are the initial functions related to (1.3).

The ‘+’ sign in (1.6) and (1.7) indicates that the data are associated with the non-negative solutions of the models (1.2) and (1.3), respectively. Physically speaking, the symbol ω\omega in equation (1.6) denotes the unidentified smooth domain within Ω\Omega, while the ω\omega referenced in (1.7) signifies the region of the irregular polyhedral inclusion present in the space of Ω\Omega. Therefore, the inverse problems (1.6) and (1.7) focus on recovering the location, shape, and parameter configuration of this anomaly. This is also known as the inverse inclusion problem in the theory of inverse problems.

Pertaining to the inverse inclusion problems (1.6) and (1.7), we are interested in the following two unique identifiability issues:

  • •

    Can we uniquely determine ω\omega and 𝐆\mathbf{G} using the measurement map ℳω,𝐆+\mathcal{M}^{+}_{\omega,\mathbf{G}}? Specifically, if two admissible inclusions (ωk,𝐆k)(\omega_{k},\mathbf{G}_{k}) for k=1,2k=1,2 produce the same boundary measurement, does it imply that (ω1,𝐆1)=(ω2,𝐆2)(\omega_{1},\mathbf{G}_{1})=(\omega_{2},\mathbf{G}_{2})? In other words, if ℳω1,𝐆1+=ℳω2,𝐆2+\mathcal{M}^{+}_{\omega_{1},\mathbf{G}_{1}}=\mathcal{M}^{+}_{\omega_{2},\mathbf{G}_{2}} in (1.2), does it follow that (ω1,𝐆1)=(ω2,𝐆2)(\omega_{1},\mathbf{G}_{1})=(\omega_{2},\mathbf{G}_{2})?

  • •

    Can we uniquely determine ω\omega and 𝐅\mathbf{F} using the measurement map ℳω,𝐅+\mathcal{M}^{+}_{\omega,\mathbf{F}}? Specifically, if two admissible inclusions (ωk,𝐅k)(\omega_{k},\mathbf{F}_{k}) for k=1,2k=1,2 produce the same boundary measurement, does it imply that (ω1,𝐅1)=(ω2,𝐅2)(\omega_{1},\mathbf{F}_{1})=(\omega_{2},\mathbf{F}_{2})? In other words, if ℳω1,𝐅1+=ℳω2,𝐅2+\mathcal{M}^{+}_{\omega_{1},\mathbf{F}_{1}}=\mathcal{M}^{+}_{\omega_{2},\mathbf{F}_{2}} in (1.3), does it follow that (ω1,𝐅1)=(ω2,𝐅2)(\omega_{1},\mathbf{F}_{1})=(\omega_{2},\mathbf{F}_{2})?

Formally, our main results can be summarized as follows:

Theorem 1.1.

Consider a certain general scenario in which an unknown smooth heterogeneity ω\omega is present within a larger domain Ω\Omega. In this scenario, the domain ω\omega and its corresponding parameter configurations 𝐆\mathbf{G} can be uniquely determined by the boundary measurement ℳω,𝐆+\mathcal{M}^{+}_{\omega,\mathbf{G}}.

Theorem 1.2.

Consider a certain general scenario where there exists an anomalous smooth or non-smooth polyhedral inclusion ω⋐Ω\omega\Subset\Omega, such that 𝐅\mathbf{F} exhibits a jump discontinuity due to adherence to certain admissibility properties. In this case, ω\omega and its parameter configurations 𝐅\mathbf{F} are uniquely determined by the boundary measurement ℳω,𝐅+\mathcal{M}^{+}_{\omega,\mathbf{F}}.

The specifics regarding the anomalous inclusion ω\omega and the admissible class of the unknowns 𝐆\mathbf{G} and 𝐅\mathbf{F} will be detailed in subsection 2.1 and 3.2. The main results of this work are contained in Theorems 2.4 and 3.4.

1.3 Technical developments and discussion

This work establishes a novel theoretical framework for solving inverse problems in complex multi-species cross-diffusion predator-prey chemotaxis ecological systems, with a focus on the unique identification of internal habitat anomalies – unknown subdomains where environmental conditions differ sharply from the surrounding region. Departing from prior studies where ecological parameters are assumed to vary smoothly or remain globally constant [6, 17], a key contribution of this paper is the detection and characterization of anomalies that manifest as jump discontinuities in the reaction functions 𝐅\mathbf{F} or 𝐆\mathbf{G}, using only exterior boundary measurements. This capability enables the non-invasive localization of degraded zones, resource hotspots, or physical barriers within a habitat – an essential task in ecological monitoring, with direct applications ranging from invasive species management to the assessment of environmental contamination.

The mathematical detection of such internal anomalies in ecological inverse problems remains largely unexplored. While related efforts exist in fields such as source reconstruction in bioluminescence tomography [5] or singular geometry recovery in mean field games [24], our study addresses the more general and ecologically relevant case of regions with potentially irregular (polyhedral) boundaries, which better approximate real-world habitat features. Furthermore, unlike our earlier works on nonlinear parabolic systems [17, 16], we relax global regularity assumptions, explicitly allowing 𝐅\mathbf{F} and 𝐆\mathbf{G} to exhibit discontinuities across an unknown interface ∂ω\partial\omega. This permits the simultaneous recovery of both the discontinuous coefficient and the geometric shape of the anomaly itself – a considerably more challenging and ecologically meaningful problem.

Beyond handling discontinuities, our framework also delivers strong identifiability results for smoother configurations, all achieved through boundary measurements. These advances are significant for two principal reasons. First, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to address the shape determination of general subdomains within a multi-species chemotaxis-predator-prey model from boundary measurements. Second, we judiciously incorporate a priori ecological information by considering admissible classes of functional responses 𝐆\mathbf{G} that are sufficiently broad to encompass physically realistic scenarios. For smoother anomalies, we require only that the unknown subdomain possesses at least C2C^{2}-regular boundaries.

A distinctive feature of our model is its capacity to capture the dynamics of multiple interacting species and chemical signals, providing a more realistic representation of complex ecological networks than traditional two-species models. This multi-species, multi-chemical framework introduces substantial analytical challenges, as couplings between population densities and chemotactic gradients create a highly nonlinear and interdependent system. It is precisely within this intricate setting—where conventional simplification techniques often fail—that we successfully solve the inverse problem of determining habitat anomalies. Our results demonstrate that even under complex ecological interactions, the discontinuous topological structure of a habitat and its associated reaction functions can be uniquely and simultaneously identified from limited boundary data. This achievement underscores the robustness of our theoretical framework and significantly extends the applicability of inverse problem methodologies to realistically complex biological systems.

This advancement is not only mathematically novel but also ecologically critical, grounded in the integrative, cross-scale nature of the model. While forward modeling of chemotaxis-predator-prey dynamics is well-developed [14, 25, 35, 30, 11, 10, 36, 9, 29, 21, 3], the corresponding inverse problem – recovering internal habitat structures from boundary data – remains largely open. In contrast to existing inverse studies in population dynamics, which have largely focused on recovering smooth coefficients under global continuity assumptions [6, 17, 23, 16, 20, 18], the present work pioneers a fundamentally distinct direction: the simultaneous geometric recovery of an unknown habitat anomaly ω\omega and the discontinuous ecological parameters governing it. This represents a critical methodological shift, moving from the question of how species interact to that of where the environment itself changes abruptly. By bridging this gap, our work provides a complete mathematical framework for linking microscale environmental heterogeneity to macroscale ecological sensing via boundary measurements.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we present the main result and detailed proof for determining smooth internal anomalies and their associated coefficient functions. In Section 3, we address the non-smooth case for the stationary chemotaxis-predator-prey system.

2 Smooth Internal Topological Structures

It is clear that if UU satisfies these four conditions, it can be expanded into a power series

U⁡(x,t,p,q)=∑m,n=1∞Um​n​(x,t)​pm​qn(m+n)!.U(x,t,p,q)=\sum\limits^{\infty}_{m,n=1}U_{mn}(x,t)\frac{p^{m}q^{n}}{(m+n)!}.

where Um​n​(x,t)=∂m∂pm​∂n∂qn​U​(x,t,𝐮0,𝟎)∈C2+α,1+α2​(E×ℝ)U_{mn}(x,t)=\frac{\partial^{m}}{\partial p^{m}}\frac{\partial^{n}}{\partial q^{n}}U(x,t,\mathbf{u}_{0},\mathbf{0})\in C^{2+\alpha,1+\frac{\alpha}{2}}(E\times\mathbb{R}).

The admissibility condition is initially imposed on UU as a prerequisite. To fulfill this condition, we extend these functions from real variables to the complex plane, resulting in U~\tilde{U}, and assume that they possess holomorphic properties with respect to the complex variables (p,q)(p,q). Afterwards, UU is obtained by restricting U~\tilde{U} to the real line. Moreover, since the values of UU lie in ℝ\mathbb{R}, we can assume that the series expansion of U~\tilde{U} is real-valued. Given the well-established physical relevance of the multi-species, multi-chemical predator-prey chemotaxis model, solutions to (1.2) are assured. With this foundation, we now define the admissible class for the coefficient function 𝐆\mathbf{G} appearing in (1.2).

Definition 2.2.

Let Ω\Omega be an open bounded set in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, such that ∂Ω∈C2\partial\Omega\in C^{2}. We say that G⁡(x,t,𝐮,𝐯)∈L2​(Ω×ℝ×ℝN×ℝM)G(x,t,\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\in L^{2}(\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{N}\times\mathbb{R}^{M}) is admissible and denoted by G∈ℬG\in\mathcal{B}, if:

  1. (i)

    GG is of the form G⁡(x,t,𝐮,𝐯)=G0​(x,t,𝐮,𝐯)+(G1​(x,t,𝐮,𝐯)−G0​(x,t,𝐮,𝐯))​χω,x∈Ω,G(x,t,\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=G^{0}(x,t,\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})+(G^{1}(x,t,\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})-G^{0}(x,t,\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}))\chi_{\omega},\ x\in\Omega, such that G1∈ℬωG^{1}\in\mathcal{B}_{\omega}, G0∈ℬΩ\ωG^{0}\in\mathcal{B}_{\Omega\backslash\omega},

  2. (ii)

    ω⋐Ω\omega\Subset\Omega is an open bounded subset such that ∂ω∈C2\partial\omega\in C^{2}, and Ω\ω\Omega\backslash\omega is connected,

  3. (iii)

    G0​(x,t,𝐮,𝐯)≢G1​(x,t,𝐮,𝐯)G^{0}(x,t,\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\not\equiv G^{1}(x,t,\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) on ∂ω×(0,T)\partial\omega\times(0,T).

Remark 2.3.

One notable distinction is that, unlike the constraints imposed on the admissible classes for coefficients in [17], we do not require their linearized counterparts to be strictly constant. This relaxation is more consistent with the physical background of the problem.

For the recovery of the smooth space ω\omega, we have (𝐮1,𝐯1)(\mathbf{u}^{1},\mathbf{v}^{1}) and (𝐮0,𝐯0)(\mathbf{u}^{0},\mathbf{v}^{0}) satisfy:

Theorem 2.4.

Let ω⋐Ω\omega\Subset\Omega be such that ω,Ω\omega,\Omega are open bounded sets in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with C2C^{2} boundary. Suppose 𝐆∈ℬ\mathbf{G}\in\mathcal{B} is such that (𝐮1,𝐯1)(\mathbf{u}^{1},\mathbf{v}^{1}) and (𝐮0,𝐯0)(\mathbf{u}^{0},\mathbf{v}^{0}) are classical solutions to (2.1) and (2.2) respectively. Then 𝐆\mathbf{G} is uniquely determined by the measurement ℳω,𝐆+\mathcal{M}^{+}_{\omega,\mathbf{G}}, in the sense that the smooth domain ω\omega and coefficient function 𝐆⁡(x,t,𝐮,𝐯)|∂ω\left.\mathbf{G}(x,t,\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\right|_{\partial\omega} are uniquely determined.

2.3 High-order variation method

Before proving Theorem 2.4, we introduce the high-order linearization technique. This method enables the reduction of the nonlinear inverse problem to a sequence of linear problems while simultaneously preserving the non-negativity constraint inherent to the model.

Taking 𝐆∈ℬE\mathbf{G}\in\mathcal{B}_{E} for some compact subset EE of Ω\Omega. Let 𝐮:(u1,…,uN)\mathbf{u}:(u_{1},\dots,u_{N}), 𝐯:=(v1,…,vM)\mathbf{v}:=(v_{1},\dots,v_{M}). With a set of initial functions 𝐮0\mathbf{u}_{0} and 𝐯0\mathbf{v}_{0}, along with a sufficiently small positive constant ε\varepsilon, we can express the functions 𝐟⁡(x,ε)\mathbf{f}(x;\varepsilon) and 𝐠⁡(x,ε)\mathbf{g}(x;\varepsilon) as follows:

and

Similarly, when 𝐯0=𝟎\mathbf{v}_{0}=\mathbf{0}, we require 𝐠1≥0\mathbf{g}_{1}\geq 0.

3 Non-smooth Internal Topological Anomalies for the Stationary Predator-Prey Chemotaxis Model

Next, we investigates internal anomalies characterized by non-smooth boundaries. We first delineate the geometric configuration of the anomalies, then introduce the necessary admissible classes of parameters or domains, and state our main theoretical findings. The corresponding detailed proofs are deferred to subsections 3.4 and 3.5.

We extend the generalization of Lemma 2.1 from [4] to dimensions n≥2n\geq 2. Our extension encompasses general corners centered at xcx_{c}, which may not necessarily be located at the origin. Moreover, our approach differs from Lemma 2.2 in [24], in which a convex conic cones was considered rather than polyhedral cones.

3.2 Admissible classes

Definition 3.2.

Let (𝐮0,𝐯0)(\mathbf{u}_{0},\mathbf{v}_{0}) be a known non-negative constant solution of (1.3), and EE be a compact subset of Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}. We say that U⁡(x,p,q):E×ℂN×ℂM→ℂU(x,p,q):E\times\mathbb{C}^{N}\times\mathbb{C}^{M}\to\mathbb{C} is admissible, denoted by U∈𝒜E,U\in\mathcal{A}_{E}, if:

  1. (i)

    The map (p,q)↦U⁡(⋅,p,q)(p,q)\mapsto U(\cdot,p,q) is holomorphic with value in C2+α​(E)C^{2+\alpha}(E) for some α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1),

  2. (ii)

    U⁡(x,⋅,⋅)U(x,\cdot,\cdot) is Cσ1,σ2C^{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}}-continuous with respect to x∈Ex\in E for some σ1,σ2∈(0,1)\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\in(0,1),

  3. (iii)

    U⁡(x,𝐮0,𝟎)=0U(x,\mathbf{u}_{0},\mathbf{0})=0 for all x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, for any 𝐮0≠0\mathbf{u}_{0}\neq 0,

  4. (iv)

    U(0,1)(x,⋅,𝐯0)=U(1,0)(x,𝐮0,⋅)=0U^{(0,1)}(x,\cdot,\mathbf{v}_{0})=U^{(1,0)}(x,\mathbf{u}_{0},\cdot)=0 for all x∈E,x\in E,

It is clear that if UU satisfies these four conditions, it can be expanded into a power series

U⁡(x,p,q)=∑m,n=1∞Um​n​(x)​pm​qn(m+n)!.U(x,p,q)=\sum\limits^{\infty}_{m,n=1}U_{mn}(x)\frac{p^{m}q^{n}}{(m+n)!}.

where Um​n​(x)=∂m∂pm​∂n∂qn​U​(x,𝐮0,𝟎)∈C2+α​(E)U_{mn}(x)=\frac{\partial^{m}}{\partial p^{m}}\frac{\partial^{n}}{\partial q^{n}}U(x,\mathbf{u}_{0},\mathbf{0})\in C^{2+\alpha}(E).

Once again, the admissibility condition is initially imposed on UU as a prerequisite. To fulfill this condition, we extend these functions from real variables to the complex plane, resulting in U~\tilde{U}, and assume that they possess holomorphic properties with respect to the complex variables (p,q)(p,q). Afterwards, UU is obtained by restricting U~\tilde{U} to the real line. Moreover, since the values of UU lie in ℝ\mathbb{R}, we can assume that the series expansion of U~\tilde{U} is real-valued.

Consider a bounded Lipschitz polyhedral domain ω⋐Ω\omega\Subset\Omega satisfying the condition that Ω\ω¯\Omega\backslash\bar{\omega} is connected, and each corner of ω\omega is a convex cone 𝒮xc,θc\mathcal{S}_{x_{c},\theta_{c}}, as defined in Subsection 3.1. Due to the strong physical significance of the multi-species-multi-chemical predator-prey chemotaxis model, solutions exist for (1.3). Consequently, we can determine the admissibility class for the coefficient function 𝐅\mathbf{F}.

Definition 3.3.

We say that F⁡(x,u1,…,uN,v1,…,vM):Ω×ℝN+M→ℝF(x,u_{1},\dots,u_{N},v_{1},\dots,v_{M}):\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^{N+M}\to\mathbb{R} is admissible, denoted by F∈𝒜F\in\mathcal{A}, if FF is of the form

F⁡(x,𝐮,𝐯)=F0​(x,𝐮,𝐯)+(F1​(x,𝐮,𝐯)−F0​(x,𝐮,𝐯))​χω,x∈Ω,F(x,\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=F^{0}(x,\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})+(F^{1}(x,\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})-F^{0}(x,\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}))\chi_{\omega},\quad x\in\Omega,

such that F1∈𝒜ωF^{1}\in\mathcal{A}_{\omega}, F0∈𝒜Ω\ωF^{0}\in\mathcal{A}_{\Omega\backslash\omega}, and for some ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N}, the ℓ\ell-th Taylor coefficient of F1F^{1} and F0F^{0}, denoted by F1​(ℓ)​(x,𝐮,𝐯)F^{1(\ell)}(x,\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) and F0​(ℓ)​(x,𝐮,𝐯)F^{0(\ell)}(x,\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) respectively, are Cσ1C^{\sigma_{1}} and Cσ0C^{\sigma_{0}} Hölder-continuous for some σ1,σ0∈(0,1)\sigma_{1},\sigma_{0}\in(0,1) with respect to x∈ωx\in\omega and x∈Ω\ωx\in\Omega\backslash\omega respectively, and in an open neighbourhood UU of ∂ω\partial\omega, F1​(ℓ)​(U∩ω)≠F0​(ℓ)​(U∩(Ω\ω))F^{1(\ell)}(U\cap\omega)\neq F^{0(\ell)}(U\cap(\Omega\backslash\omega)).

It is worth noting that the admissibility condition we consider differs from those in previous works on biology models, such as [17, 20, 23, 6], where the authors assume that the coefficient function FF is analytic in the entire real space ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. In our case, we adopt a more general approach, allowing for singularities at the boundary ∂E\partial E of compact subsets EE of Ω\Omega.

3.3 Main theorem

Having established these definitions, we now present the principal results of this subsection. Specifically, we demonstrate that, microlocally within a corner 𝒦h\mathcal{K}_{h} of the domain ω\omega, the solution pairs (𝐮1,𝐯1)(\mathbf{u}^{1},\mathbf{v}^{1}) and (𝐮0,𝐯0)(\mathbf{u}^{0},\mathbf{v}^{0}) in the habitat adopt the forms as:

for i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N and j=1,…,Mj=1,\dots,M.

We next state our main results.

Theorem 3.4.

Suppose that 𝐅∈𝒜\mathbf{F}\in\mathcal{A} and ω⋐Ω\omega\Subset\Omega is a convex polyhedron. Assume that (𝐮1,𝐯1)(\mathbf{u}^{1},\mathbf{v}^{1}) and (𝐮0,𝐯0)(\mathbf{u}^{0},\mathbf{v}^{0}) are classical solutions to (3.23) and (3.24) respectively. Then ω\omega and 𝐅\mathbf{F} are uniquely determined by the boundary measurement ℳω,𝐅+\mathcal{M}^{+}_{\omega,\mathbf{F}}.

Drawing from this theorem, we derive two corollaries. When each corner within the polyhedral domain ω\omega takes the form of a convex conic cone 𝒮⊂Ω\mathcal{S}\subset\Omega, characterized by

𝒮:={y∈Ω:0≤∠(y−xc,vc)≤θc,θc∈(0,π/2)},\mathcal{S}:=\{y\in\Omega:0\leq\angle(y-x_{c},v_{c})\leq\theta_{c},\theta_{c}\in(0,\pi/2)\},

where xcx_{c} represents the apex, vcv_{c} signifies the axis, and the opening angle is 2​θc∈(0,π)2\theta_{c}\in(0,\pi). By defining a new admissible class 𝒞\mathcal{C} akin to Definition 3.3, Corollary 3.5 affirms the following:

Corollary 3.5.

Suppose that 𝐅∈𝒞\mathbf{F}\in\mathcal{C} and ω⋐Ω\omega\Subset\Omega is a convex domain with conic corners. Assume that (𝐮1,𝐯1)(\mathbf{u}^{1},\mathbf{v}^{1}) and (𝐮0,𝐯0)(\mathbf{u}^{0},\mathbf{v}^{0}) are classical solutions to (3.23) and (3.24) respectively. Then ω\omega and 𝐅\mathbf{F} are uniquely determined by the boundary measurement ℳω,𝐅+\mathcal{M}^{+}_{\omega,\mathbf{F}}.

The verification for this assertion follows as in the proof of the main theorem, by replacing Lemma 3.1 with the corresponding one for conic corners (the proof of which can be found in Lemma 2.2 of [24]).

The second corollary asserts that if ω⋐Ω\omega\Subset\Omega is a smooth domain, the result follows directly from the time-dependent case and it is feasible to retrieve the anomaly and coefficient functions:

Corollary 3.6.

Suppose that 𝐅∈𝒜\mathbf{F}\in\mathcal{A}. Let ω⋐Ω\omega\Subset\Omega be such that ω,Ω\omega,\Omega are open bounded sets in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with C2C^{2} boundary. Assume that (𝐮1,𝐯1)(\mathbf{u}^{1},\mathbf{v}^{1}) and (𝐮0,𝐯0)(\mathbf{u}^{0},\mathbf{v}^{0}) are classical solutions to (3.23) and (3.24) respectively. Then the smooth domain ω\omega and the coefficient function 𝐅\mathbf{F} are uniquely determined by the boundary measurement ℳω,𝐅+\mathcal{M}^{+}_{\omega,\mathbf{F}}.

This is a direct result of Theorem 2.4, since the dynamic establishment naturally extends to the corresponding equilibrium state under the assumption of Theorem 2.4.

One intriguing observation is the presence of two distinct scenarios when 𝐅=0\mathbf{F}=0 within ω\omega or when 𝐅=0\mathbf{F}=0 outside of ω\omega. In the former case, ω\omega signifies habitat degradation where no species can survive. In contrast, in the latter case, ω\omega may represent an enclosed area, suggesting a high likelihood of animals being confined or microorganisms akin to those in a petri dish.

3.4 Recovery of the polyhedral domain

In this subsection, we prove Theorem 3.4, beginning with the recovery of the polyhedral domain. First, we introduce a key auxiliary lemma; its proof follows that of Theorem 4.1 in [24], adapted to the case of polyhedral corners.

And we can apply the same method to address the case where Fui​uim⁡(I​I)F^{m(II)}_{u_{i}u_{i}} is unknown for i=2,…,Ni=2,\dots,N.

Under this assumption, (3.33) becomes:

{−d1​Δ​u11​(I​I)−F1,u1​u11​(I​I)​(u1​(I))2=−d1​Δ​u10​(I​I)−F1,u1​u10​(I​I)​(u1​(I))2=0 in ​𝒦h,u11​(I​I)​(x)=u10​(I​I)​(x) on ​∂𝒦h\∂Bh.\begin{cases}-d_{1}\Delta u^{1(II)}_{1}-F^{1(II)}_{1,u_{1}u_{1}}(u^{1(I)})^{2}=-d_{1}\Delta u^{0(II)}_{1}-F^{0(II)}_{1,u_{1}u_{1}}(u^{1(I)})^{2}=0&\quad\text{ in }\mathcal{K}_{h},\\ u_{1}^{1(II)}(x)=u_{1}^{0(II)}(x)&\quad\text{ on }\partial\mathcal{K}_{h}\backslash\partial B_{h}.\end{cases} (3.34)

Denote wn​(x)=u1n⁡(I​I)​(x)​(n=0,1)w_{n}(x)=u^{n(II)}_{1}(x)(n=0,1), P=0P=0, qn=F1,u1​u1n⁡(I​I)q_{n}=F^{n(II)}_{1,u_{1}u_{1}} and h⁡(x)=(u11​(I))2​(x)h(x)=(u^{1(I)}_{1})^{2}(x), (3.34) can be transformed into (3.26). If

F1,u1​u11,1​(I​I)​(xc)≠F1,u1​u10​(I​I)​(xc),F^{1,1(II)}_{1,u_{1}u_{1}}(x_{c})\neq F^{0(II)}_{1,u_{1}u_{1}}(x_{c}),

Similarly, if Fuk​uhm⁡(I​I)F^{m(II)}_{u_{k}u_{h}} (k≠h)(k\neq h) has a jump singularity, we can select 𝐮~m⁡(I)\tilde{\mathbf{u}}^{m(I)} which has non-trivial element only at the hh and kk positions. And we take 𝐮~m⁡(I)=(1,1,0,⋯,0)\tilde{\mathbf{u}}^{m(I)}=(1,1,0,\cdots,0) as an example. Now (3.33) becomes

{−d1​Δ​u11​(I​I)−2​F1,u1​u21,1​(I​I)​u11​(I)​u21​(I)=−d1​Δ​u10​(I​I)−2​F1,u1​u20​(I​I)​u11​(I)​u21​(I)=0 in ​𝒦h,u11​(I​I)​(x)=u10​(I​I)​(x) on ​∂𝒦h\∂Bh.\begin{cases}-d_{1}\Delta u^{1(II)}_{1}-2F^{1,1(II)}_{1,u_{1}u_{2}}u^{1(I)}_{1}u^{1(I)}_{2}=-d_{1}\Delta u^{0(II)}_{1}-2F^{0(II)}_{1,u_{1}u_{2}}u^{1(I)}_{1}u^{1(I)}_{2}=0&\quad\text{ in }\mathcal{K}_{h},\\ u_{1}^{1(II)}(x)=u_{1}^{0(II)}(x)&\quad\text{ on }\partial\mathcal{K}_{h}\backslash\partial B_{h}.\end{cases}

However, we have chosen the initial function f1,1​(x)f_{1,1}(x) and f1,2​(x)f_{1,2}(x) in such a way that based on the maximum principle for the elliptic equation, neither u11​(I)=0u^{1(I)}_{1}=0 nor u21​(I)=0u^{1(I)}_{2}=0 holds on ∂ω1⊃∂𝒦\partial\omega_{1}\supset\partial\mathcal{K}. This leads to a contradiction, implying that ω1=ω2\omega_{1}=\omega_{2}. Thus, we have once again established the uniqueness of ω\omega uniquely.

Hence we can uniquely determine ω\omega if any of the second-order coefficients of 𝐅\mathbf{F} has a jump singularity. However, if all the second-order coefficient functions are identical at the point xcx_{c}, then ui1​(I​I)​(x)=ui0​(I​I)​(x)u^{1(II)}_{i}(x)=u^{0(II)}_{i}(x) on ∂ω1\partial\omega_{1} for each ii and u~i1​(I​I)∈C2+α​(Ω)\tilde{u}^{1(II)}_{i}\in C^{2+\alpha}(\Omega). In this case, the argument must be extended to higher-order variations. To analyze higher-order Taylor coefficients of 𝐅\mathbf{F}, we consider the linearized systems of order ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N}, with ll-th order variations defined by

ui(ℓ)(x):=∂εℓui|ε=0,vj(ℓ)(x):=∂εℓvj|ε=0for i=1,…,N;j=1,…,M.u_{i}^{(\ell)}(x):=\partial_{\varepsilon}^{\ell}u_{i}|_{\varepsilon=0},\ v_{j}^{(\ell)}(x):=\partial_{\varepsilon}^{\ell}v_{j}|_{\varepsilon=0}\quad\text{for }i=1,\dots,N;j=1,\dots,M.

This recursive approach yields a sequence of systems, each of which can be applied again when a discontinuity is present in the corresponding higher-order Taylor coefficient 𝐅(ℓ)\mathbf{F}^{(\ell)}.

We proceed with the case ℓ=3\ell=3. Under the assumptions above, the equality of measurement maps ℳω1,𝐅1=ℳω2,𝐅2\mathcal{M}_{\omega_{1},\mathbf{F}^{1}}=\mathcal{M}_{\omega_{2},\mathbf{F}^{2}} implies ui1,1​(I​I)=ui0​(I​I)u^{1,1(II)}_{i}=u^{0(II)}_{i} on ∂ω\partial\omega. Since the first- and second-order terms ui1​(I),ui1​(I​I)​(i=1,…,N)u^{1(I)}_{i},u^{1(II)}_{i}(i=1,\dots,N) are now fixed and smooth, the system governing the third-order variations uin⁡(I​I​I),uin⁡(I​I​I)​(n=0,1)u^{n(III)}_{i},u^{n(III)}_{i}(n=0,1) reduces to an elliptic equation whose remaining terms depend only on these lower-order solutions. Consequently, the unique continuation principle for elliptic equations applies once more, leading to a system of the form (3.26) with sufficiently regular coefficients. A contradiction again arises if the third-order coefficients of 𝐅\mathbf{F} possess a jump singularity, thereby uniquely determining ω\omega.

The argument for orders ℓ⁡(ℓ≥4)\ell(\ell\geq 4) follows identically. Hence, ω\omega is uniquely determined whenever 𝐅\mathbf{F} has a jump singularity. Conversely, if 𝐅\mathbf{F} does not have a jump singularity, by definition, no such ω\omega exists.

The proof is complete.

3.5 Recovery of the coefficient functions

Having established the unique identifiability result for the intrinsic structure of anomalies in the given biological model, we proceed to consider the recovery for the coefficient function 𝐅\mathbf{F}. In this subsection, we keep the notations in (3.27), (3.28) and (3.29).

Repeating the argument above, from the first order linearisation (3.31), ui1​(I)u^{1(I)}_{i}, ui2​(I)u^{2(I)}_{i} satisfy the following equations

{−di​Δ​ui1​(I)​(x)=−di​Δ​ui2​(I)​(x)=0 in ​𝒦h,∂νu11​(I)​(x)=∂νu12​(I)​(x) on ​∂𝒦h\∂Bh,u11​(I)​(x)=u12​(I)​(x) on ​∂𝒦h\∂Bh,u11​(I)​(x)=u12​(I)​(x)=f1,1​(x)>0 on ​∂Ω.\begin{cases}-d_{i}\Delta u^{1(I)}_{i}(x)=-d_{i}\Delta u^{2(I)}_{i}(x)=0&\quad\text{ in }\mathcal{K}_{h},\\ \partial_{\nu}u^{1(I)}_{1}(x)=\partial_{\nu}u^{2(I)}_{1}(x)&\quad\text{ on }\partial\mathcal{K}_{h}\backslash\partial B_{h},\\ u^{1(I)}_{1}(x)=u^{2(I)}_{1}(x)&\quad\text{ on }\partial\mathcal{K}_{h}\backslash\partial B_{h},\\ u^{1(I)}_{1}(x)=u^{2(I)}_{1}(x)=f_{1,1}(x)>0&\quad\text{ on }\partial\Omega.\end{cases}

Given the positivity of the initial function f1,if_{1,i}, we can infer the positivity of u¯i(I)​(x)\bar{u}^{(I)}_{i}(x) for each ii.

To recover the second-order of the unknown coefficient function 𝐅\mathbf{F}, we need to proceed to the system for ui1​(I​I)u^{1(II)}_{i} and ui2​(I​I)u^{2(II)}_{i}, which satisfies:

{−d1​Δ​u11​(I​I)−2​F1,u1​u21,1​(I​I)​u¯11​(I)​u¯21​(I)=−d1​Δ​u12​(I​I)−2​F1,u1​u22,1​(I​I)​u¯11​(I)​u¯21​(I)=0 in ​𝒦h,u11​(I​I)​(x)=u12​(I​I)​(x) on ​∂𝒦h\∂Bh.\begin{cases}-d_{1}\Delta u^{1(II)}_{1}-2F^{1,1(II)}_{1,u_{1}u_{2}}\bar{u}^{1(I)}_{1}\bar{u}^{1(I)}_{2}=-d_{1}\Delta u^{2(II)}_{1}-2F^{2,1(II)}_{1,u_{1}u_{2}}\bar{u}^{1(I)}_{1}\bar{u}^{1(I)}_{2}=0&\quad\text{ in }\mathcal{K}_{h},\\ u_{1}^{1(II)}(x)=u_{1}^{2(II)}(x)&\quad\text{ on }\partial\mathcal{K}_{h}\backslash\partial B_{h}.\end{cases}
